name: Daria Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work with the independent Work Futures Panel. We do not work for AI firms, employers, unions or government, and this is confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 27 and lead nine revenue analysts for a large hotel group. We set room prices, check booking patterns and call hotel managers when a conference suddenly fills a week. I have an MBA and earn well for this job because I know how to turn a quiet property around. I use AI tools every day for forecasts and first drafts, then I make the pricing call.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my fiancé, who runs a small bicycle repair shop. We have almost a year of household expenses saved, partly because his shop income moves with the seasons. There are plenty of hotel and retail management jobs here, but I like building a business that can pay its own way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my analysts AI Plateau is already close to how we work. A better forecast is useful, but a room price has to make sense to the hotel manager who sees the guests.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my role stays strong. A small tool saves a little checking time, while the real work is noticing a festival, a cancelled meeting or a broken lift before the numbers settle. My fiancé’s repair shop could still have a slow winter, so I keep an eye on our household reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d continue the Monday price call with hotel managers and keep comparing AI forecasts with their local bookings. If a minor new feature arrives, I’d test it on last spring’s conference weeks before changing live prices. We would keep transferring a set amount into savings from my paycheck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my own job and income. We have nearly a year saved, and no sudden change is coming in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Give me a case the forecast missed.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A hotel beside the exhibition hall sold out after a small trade fair changed dates. The booking curve looked ordinary until the organiser called the front desk. I moved the price the next morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your fiancé’s winter is slow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His shop has been through slow months before. We pay the fixed bills from my salary and let the reserve cover a short gap if needed. We do not raise room prices to solve our household worries.

say: **AI Plateau** makes familiar forecasts a little more useful.
Hotel managers still bring **local news** that changes room prices.
think: My pricing role looks **secure** under modest change.
My fiancé’s **repair shop** may still have a slow winter.
do: **Keep** Monday price calls with hotel managers.
**Test** a minor feature on last spring conference weeks before live use.
**Continue** transferring a set amount from each paycheck into savings.
feel: I feel **calm** about work and household income.
S0.quote: We do not raise room prices to solve our household worries.
fieldNote: Her **near-year reserve** and high salary cover seasonal shop swings without changing hotel prices for personal reasons.
She uses AI **daily** but looks for local booking news before setting a price.

steps.text: Keep Monday room-price calls with hotel managers
Test the forecast feature on old conference weeks before live prices
Transfer a set amount from each paycheck into household savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will automate more pricing, booking replies and schedule checks. If the company saves money, it should give people a clear chance to earn a different role before cutting them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, much of my day is screen work the new tools can do. I might be asked to supervise more hotels with fewer analysts, and a company could decide it needs fewer revenue leads too. I have other local options and savings, but I would not assume my current pay is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d run a pilot with three hotels, asking managers to record when they reject AI price advice. I’d take the paid forecasting-system course if my director offers a place. If lead posts shrink after rollout, I’d apply for open hotel general-manager trainee roles only if the salary covers our fixed bills while my fiancé’s shop varies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about my pay and my team. I can show where the forecast fails, but I cannot vote on how many lead jobs the group keeps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why general management?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want to understand staffing, repairs and guest problems at one building, not only price its rooms. A trainee title would be a step back, so I would read the pay and duties carefully. I would not leave the revenue desk for a hotel manager title alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you bring in the union?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would first ask the director for a written redeployment plan and let employees decide how to represent themselves. I believe firms can change a business when they must. They should keep the promises they make to staff while doing it.

say: **Pricing tools** may change jobs; staff need a clear route to other roles.
I’d show managers’ **rejected prices** alongside the pilot results.
think: I could supervise more hotels with **fewer analysts**, which may also reduce the number of lead posts.
My current **pay** may fall if revenue-lead posts shrink, even though other hotels are hiring.
do: **Pilot** the system at three hotels and record manager overrides.
**Take** paid forecasting training if offered a place.
**Apply** for hotel manager trainee openings only if salary covers fixed bills.
feel: I feel **anxious** about lead posts and household pay.
S1.quote: I would not leave the revenue desk for a hotel manager title alone.
fieldNote: She uses a **three-hotel pilot** to test whether AI prices survive local manager checks.
Her **career switch** depends on real trainee pay because her fiancé’s shop income is seasonal.

steps.text: Pilot AI pricing at three hotels and record manager overrides
Take paid forecasting-system training if the director offers a place
Apply for hotel manager trainee roles only if salary covers fixed bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell staff AGI by 2028 could set prices, answer booking questions and plan our work as well as we do. Hotels should tell employees when decisions will be made, not ask them to smile through a secret cut list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Full thinking AI by 2028 could remove most of my desk role before capable robots reach hands-on hotel jobs around 2031. I expect revenue teams to shrink, and I might lose the lead salary. With almost a year of savings and other hotels nearby, I can search, but the shock would still be personal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I’d ask the group director for the staffing timetable and a list of open property roles. I’d calculate the minimum salary our rent and the bicycle shop need, then apply for two posted hotel operations jobs if they meet that floor. If AGI arrives in 2028 and I’m cut, I’d accept a real property job only after checking its duties and pay with my fiancé.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about losing the work I am proud of. I am not panicking; our reserve gives me time to refuse an offer that would leave us short every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your fiancé?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say my revenue title might go before his repair work does. We would use the shop income and savings for bills while I looked, but we would not take on a larger shop lease in that period. My fiancé should not have to gamble the bicycle repair shop because my revenue desk changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need from the director?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decision date, severance figures and real property vacancies with pay ranges. I do not need a comforting speech. I need enough detail to compare an offer with our bills.

say: **AGI by 2028** needs staffing dates and posted property jobs.
I would ask for **pay ranges**, not a reassuring speech.
think: My desk work could go in **2028**, before hotel robots around 2031.
My lead salary is at risk, but **savings and local jobs** allow a search.
do: **Ask** for decision dates and open property posts next month.
**Calculate** our minimum salary before applying for two operations jobs.
**Decline** a larger shop lease if my revenue job ends.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing a valued role, with time to search.
S2.quote: My fiancé should not have to gamble the bicycle repair shop because my revenue desk changes.
fieldNote: She distinguishes her **2028 desk risk** from later robot changes in hands-on hotel work.
Her **salary floor** protects rent and the seasonal repair shop; the reserve buys choice, not certainty.

steps.text: Apply for two posted hotel operations jobs if salaries cover fixed bills
Postpone a larger bicycle shop lease if the revenue job ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives the group time to try people in hotel operations while they still have wages. We should tell staff what each trial pays and who will train them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough for me to learn a property’s daily work, but pricing and booking could still be taken by AGI in 2031. Robots for cleaning and other hands-on work follow around 2034; I would not pretend that gives my desk extra years. A hotel manager post might survive, but no one owes me that vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From January 2027 I’d take one paid week each quarter alongside a hotel general manager if my director approves cover for my team. I’d take an operations certificate only if the group pays and lets me study on work time. If AGI arrives around 2031, I’d apply for a property manager opening only if its pay meets our rent and shop budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy. I can use five years well, but I have to see what a manager actually does on a broken-lift morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on that morning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would call maintenance, tell the front desk which rooms are affected and offer a guest a fair alternative. Pricing knowledge helps, but I have not managed an engineer or a guest queue. I want to learn how a hotel handles a broken lift before applying to manage a hotel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the director will not release you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the revenue job and ask to shadow during a quieter week. I will not leave nine analysts with an uncovered price call. The certificate would wait until the group funds it.

say: **Five years** allows paid trials in hotel operations.
Staff need the **pay and trainer** named before a trial begins.
think: Pricing and bookings face AGI in **2031**, before cleaning robots around 2034.
A property-manager **vacancy** is possible, not promised.
do: **Shadow** a hotel general manager quarterly from January 2027 if cover is approved.
**Study** for an operations certificate only with funding and paid time.
**Apply** after 2031 for property roles only if pay covers rent and the bicycle-shop budget.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, with time to learn unfamiliar site duties.
S3.quote: I want to learn how a hotel handles a broken lift before applying to manage a hotel.
fieldNote: She names a **real skill gap** in managing repairs and guest queues despite strong pricing performance.
Every training step needs **paid time** and cover for her nine analysts.
She says **uneasy**, though the possible loss of her pricing desk puts household income at risk in 2031.

steps.text: Shadow a hotel general manager quarterly if team cover is approved
Take an operations certificate only with group funding and paid time
Apply after 2031 for property jobs only if pay covers rent and bicycle-shop budget

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives firms a decade to plan properly, and employees can use that time to build new skills without begging for unpaid leave. I would want actual hotel vacancies listed beside every training offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I could run a property or even help my fiancé expand his shop if the numbers make sense. My pricing desk still faces AGI in 2036, while hands-on hotel robots arrive around 2039. I have savings and several employers to approach, so I do not feel my income is in immediate danger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep leading revenue reviews and continue our savings transfer. I’d take a paid hotel-operations rotation if offered with my salary intact, and review property-manager jobs each year. In the first year after 2036, I’d apply for one only if the role has staff authority and enough pay; we would consider a shop expansion only after checking a year of its accounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the next few years. A decade lets me put real figures beside each choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put your savings into the shop now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My fiancé’s bicycle shop had a good summer, but that is not a full year of earnings. I would review its rent, parts costs and repeat customers before investing a deposit. My fiancé agrees that the numbers come first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a good property post include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A staff budget, authority to solve guest problems and pay that covers our household bills. I would not trade a well-paid desk for a title that cannot fix a broken lift. I would read the contract with my fiancé.

say: A **decade** should link paid training to actual hotel vacancies.
I would judge new roles by **authority and pay**.
think: My pricing desk faces AGI in **2036**, with hotel robots around 2039.
Savings and nearby employers make an immediate **income crisis** unlikely.
do: **Keep** leading revenue reviews and funding savings in 2026.
**Take** a paid operations rotation only if offered with full salary.
**Review** property-manager jobs annually before applying after 2036.
feel: I feel **calm** about the next few years with time for choices.
S4.quote: My fiancé’s bicycle shop had a good summer, but that is not a full year of earnings.
fieldNote: She weighs a possible **shop expansion** against a full year of accounts, not one strong season.
Her **ten-year route** relies on paid rotations, real vacancies and roles with staff authority.

steps.text: Keep leading hotel revenue reviews through 2026
Continue transferring part of each paycheck into household savings
Take paid hotel-operations rotation if offered with full salary
Review property-manager vacancies each year for pay and authority

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the revenue desk could be cut before I have run a hotel property. A decision date, pay ranges for real openings and a paid operations trial would help. Our savings let me search; they do not make an empty job title useful.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the hotel manager who carries the guest complaint when the price algorithm gets a busy week wrong. The software can change a number in a second. A person has to explain the bill at the front desk.

headlineQuote: A person has to explain the bill at the front desk.
portrait: **Daria, 27**, is an MBA-trained revenue manager leading nine analysts at a large hotel group.
Her **high pay**, near-year reserve and several local employers give her options; her fiancé’s bicycle shop income varies.
She uses **AI daily** for forecasts but checks hotel news and keeps final responsibility for room prices.
She is **calm** under mild change, anxious about 2028 desk cuts and methodical about paid hotel-operations trials.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut her revenue post before she has property-management experience.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **decision date**, pay ranges and a paid hotel-operations trial would help.
